title: Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind quietly working on joint AI safety body
subtitle: The three top labs have met since July to explore an industry-run standards organization — a coordination move usually reserved for regulated sectors like finance and aviation.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The Washington Post reported on September 14, 2026, that Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind have been meeting on a working-group basis since at least July to discuss forming a joint standards body for AI. Dario Amodei of Anthropic is driving the push, with Sam Altman backing it as a faster path than waiting on federal legislation. Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis had separately floated a FINRA-style Frontier AI Standards Body — modeled on the securities industry's self-regulator — in a July 14 proposal. The talks predate Amodei's Saturday essay calling on the industry to slow the pace of capability development.

The mechanism matters more than the announcement. FINRA-style bodies work in finance and aviation because member firms accept binding rules — audits, incident reporting, revoked licenses — in exchange for keeping the government at arm's length. An AI equivalent would need auditors who can actually inspect training runs, a common definition of what counts as a dangerous capability, and enforcement teeth that survive when one member disagrees with a ruling. None of those exist today, and antitrust lawyers have already flagged coordination risk if rivals write rules together without a statutory shield.

The three companies do not yet agree on scope. Anthropic wants government partnership woven in; OpenAI leans toward voluntary industry standards with selective support for state laws; Google DeepMind favors a professionalized standards organization outside government. That gap, and the White House posture — Trump on Monday called the oversight push a "SICK conspiracy" — is why the group has stayed quiet. A body announced without buy-in from Washington risks looking either like regulatory capture or like a workaround the administration will attack.

For learners: watch what these bodies define, not what they promise. A standards body that publishes a common threshold for "dangerous capability" — with pass/fail tests any lab must run before release — would be a real coordination move. One that publishes principles without tests is a press release. The distinction is the same one that separates ISO 9001 from a corporate values statement, and it is the yardstick to hold this project to when the formal announcement lands.
